newsitem.title: NEPAL: Italy's Impregilo wins Nepal hydro deal.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Impregilo wins Nepal hydro deal.

text.p: Italy's Impregilo Spa has won a $129.6 million contract to build a hydroelectric power plant in Nepal, officials said on Monday.
They said Impregilo will be responsible for the civil engineering work for the Kali Gandaki 'A' hydropower plant in western Nepal.
The work includes the construction of a diversion dam, tunnel, powerhouse and de-sanding basin for the plant, which is expected to produce 144 megawatts of electricity starting in July 2000.

"They (Impregilo) were the lowest of nine international bidders," Kirti Chand Thakur, managing director of the state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), told Reuters in the Nepali capital Kathmandu.
Japan and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) have pledged to provide $160 million each for the $453 million project. NEA will provide $133 million to cover local costs.

Thakur said two separate bids would be invited for the supply of power generating equipment, gates and valves for the plant, which will be the Himalayan kingdom's largest hydroelectric plant when it starts generating energy in 2000.
The kingdom's cascading rivers have the potential to generate up to 83,000 megawatts of power.
But Nepal, one of the world's 10 poorest countries, generates only 293 megawatts of electricity against its peak demand of 302 megawatts. Demand is growing by 10 percent every year.
Electricity is available to only 15 percent of the country's 21 million people.

The Kali Gandaki plant will operate at full capacity throughout the year, officials said. It was considered a low cost option for the kingdom although some local environmental groups had initially questioned its social impact and cost.
Industrialists say the power shortfall is a major hurdle to industrial growth and could hamper Nepal's efforts to entice foreign inviestment.
In 1995, the World Bank dropped plans to lend $175 million for a planned 201-megawatt hydroelectric plant in eastern Nepal.
The World Bank doubted Nepal's capacity to implement the $764 million Arun III plant and asked Kathmandu to develop small and medium-sized power plants.
